extracted.intended_audience: novelists, advanced fiction writers, and students of narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and applying narrative method (dramatic scene vs. narrator/conspectus) and on techniques for dramatizing inner states, implying facts, and giving weight to undramatic subjects in the novel. Uses examples (James, Flaubert, etc.) to show when to employ narrator, direct view, or purely scenic presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize undramatic subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: An undramatic, pictorial subject (a condition or situation rather than overt action) can and often should be treated dramatically so that thought and feeling 'act themselves' before the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the inner life visible by letting 'thought have its tell-tale gestures and its speaking looks' so the story is 'expressed through them' rather than summarized. Examples: Strether in The Ambassadors and Milly in The Wings of the Dove — books whose matter is 'entirely undramatic' are nevertheless rendered dramatic by this method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gratuitous dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not pepper descriptive surfaces with animated dialogue when characters 'really have nothing to contribute to the subject.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialogue used as filler cheapens future necessary speech; only let characters speak when their talk advances or enacts the subject. Anti-pattern: inserting talk merely to animate a scene without contributing to the drama or revelation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surround and imply facts rather than state them
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than walking straight up to a fact and putting it into phrases, 'surround the fact, and so detach it inviolate' — imply and suggest until the reader 'becomes possessed' of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scatter small, seemingly insignificant words or glimpses that later cohere into a complete realization for the reader. The revealing word may 'not seem peculiarly emphatic as it was uttered,' yet later supplies the knowledge — this is preferable to blunt exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use surface gestures and peripheral details to enact inner states
rubrics_metrics.description: Let small looks, pauses, hasty motions, and the 'light stir and vibration' of sensibility stand for deeper mental content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the character among others and note 'the glimpse that her friend catches' or the 'broken phrases' and setting elements (light, rain, room) that together embody motives and appeals. These enactments give solidity without explicit internal monologue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create stereoscopic solidity by viewing from multiple angles
rubrics_metrics.description: Raise a character or situation out of its setting by cutting behind it and lavishing care on peripheral aspects so the reader can 'see round the object' and the image acquires weight and a 'third dimension.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop the 'outer rim' of a consciousness: show the person in varied company and contexts so the core subject 'stands out, and casts its shadow.' This gives more substance than direct emphasis or underlining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose narrator only when he contributes value
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator (seer/recorder) should be used when his presence 'contributes definitely to the effect of the subject'; otherwise the direct view assigned to the reader is preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject 'asks for no more than to be reflected and pictured,' the narrator may be a value; but when direct, dramatic presentation is better, 'he is better dispensed with and put out of the way.' Consider economy: the narrator should serve a purpose, not be habitually present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match method to the scale and reach of the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount, extent, time-span, crowd-size and manifold nature of a subject determine whether it must be presented as pictorial/conspectus by a narrator or can be treated in pure dramatic scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large, panoramic chronicles (crowds, long time spans) 'exceed the capacity of the straight and dramatic method' and require the narrator's general view; compact, limited situations can be shown scenically without narrator intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain consistency of chosen method
rubrics_metrics.description: Once an author chooses a dominant method (pure drama, narrator-led picture, diffused subjective impression), the work should remain consistent in that method to be 'true to itself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The Awkward Age uses pure dramatic presentation throughout (no interior insight, only looks and speech) and thereby secures compactness and direct force. Mixing methods without need can dilute effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let scenes embody appeals and meanings rather than announce them
rubrics_metrics.description: Key appeals, revelations, or moral moves should emerge from the scene's elements (setting, gestures, broken phrases) rather than being stated as a declaration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the Susan Stringham visit scene, the 'cheerless little room and the falling light and Densher's uneasy movements' embody the suppressed appeal. The scene 'has embodied it; the cheerless little room ... have all contributed.' Avoid making a scene function merely as a platform for explicit statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit revelation to feel discovered by the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Clues should be presented so that a reader at one moment 'springs up complete and solid' with a piece of knowledge that earlier may have passed unnoticed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plant the enlightening word or detail unobtrusively; when the reader later recognizes it, the knowledge is more powerful than if it had been flagged repeatedly. This is preferable to explicit recapitulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the novelist's advantage over the playwright carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: When treating a story scenically the novelist can fix not only words but the manner of their utterance and the ideal acting, avoiding reliance on external interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If adopting drama, the novelist may 'ensure the very best acting imaginable' by prescribing manner and amplification in stage-direction-like prose. But this ties the novelist to playwright-like restraints — choose deliberately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply 'method upon method' to achieve complex effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Layering methods (vision of a vision; process of thinking exposed objectively) can enrich fiction and produce delicate, profound effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Henry James's use of nested perspective and dramatization ('method upon method') demonstrates opportunities for new modulations and harmonies. This is an advanced device; criticism should isolate technique from temperament to assimilate it into craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct view when the narrator offers no added value
rubrics_metrics.description: If the presence of a seer/recorder does not contribute distinctly to the subject's effect, provide a direct view of the matter for clarity and force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where 'other things are equal a direct view of the matter in hand is the best.' Reserve narrator's voice for when it economizes or adds meaning; otherwise remove intermediary commentary.
